title: The wolf and the lamb (Isaiah 11:1–9)
hook: a shoot from Jesse's root; the Church draws its seven gifts of the Spirit from this chapter

segments.voice: Yesterday, swords hammered into farm tools, and nations that will not learn war any more. Your line was ploughshares. What small war did you start to end? Day four hundred eighteen.

A stump. Nothing left of the tree but a stump, low to the ground, the kind you'd trip over. Some readers see the royal family of David in it: once a great tree, now cut down. And then, in the Douay-Rheims: "there shall come forth a rod out of the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up out of his root." A green shoot from a dead stump. Jesse was David's father, the man whose youngest son was out with the sheep. In Advent, some Catholic families hang ornaments on a Jesse tree, and this is the verse it grows from.
screen: `A STUMP, LOW TO THE GROUND.` → `A SHOOT FROM THE ROOT OF JESSE.` → `THE JESSE TREE IN ADVENT.`

segments.voice: Isaiah says what will rest on this new king. In the Douay: "the spirit of wisdom, and of understanding, the spirit of counsel, and of fortitude, the spirit of knowledge, and of godliness," and he shall be filled "with the spirit of the fear of the Lord." Count them: seven. And that's where the Church's list of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit comes from. Wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord. Readers of the Hebrew point out that it names only six: fear of the Lord appears twice. The Greek and Latin translators rendered the first one as godliness, or piety, and so the list became seven. Christians read the shoot from Jesse as Christ, on whom the Spirit rests completely. And the Catechism teaches that these same gifts are given to every Christian, sealed especially in confirmation, as steady dispositions that make a person ready to follow the Spirit's lead. Then the chapter's picture of what this king's reign looks like. "The wolf shall dwell with the lamb: and the leopard shall lie down with the kid," calf and lion together, "and a little child shall lead them." A toddler plays by a snake's hole and isn't hurt. Notice: the saying goes that the lion will lie down with the lamb. Isaiah actually pairs the wolf with the lamb, and the lion with the calf. Either way the point is the same. When the earth is full of the knowledge of the Lord, the old enemies stop hurting each other.
screen: `SEVEN SPIRITS ON THE SHOOT.` · `SIX IN HEBREW, SEVEN IN LATIN.` · `GIFTS SEALED IN CONFIRMATION.` · `THE WOLF SHALL DWELL WITH THE LAMB.` · then, large: `THE SPIRIT OF WISDOM, AND OF UNDERSTANDING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for one gift of the Spirit. Settle, and breathe. Let the seven pass slowly through your mind: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, fear of the Lord. See if one of them catches, one you could use this week. Counsel, for a decision. Fortitude, for something you dread. Understanding, for a person who baffles you. Choose it. If you pray, ask the Holy Spirit for that one gift, simply, by name. If you don't, hold the word and picture what your week would look like with more of it. The bell holds the time.
Gifts of the Holy Spirit. Seven: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety and fear of the Lord, drawn from Isaiah eleven. Today's word.
screen: `GIFTS OF THE HOLY SPIRIT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: wisdom, understanding, counsel. Today, when you hit the moment you need your chosen gift, stop and ask for it. Day four hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Catholics are sealed with the gifts of the Holy Spirit in confirmation, many families keep a Jesse tree through Advent, and Isaiah 11 is read at Mass in Advent, including the Second Sunday of Advent in one year of the cycle.

fork.setup: you're reading Isaiah 11 in Hebrew and counting the spirits that rest on the shoot of Jesse. how many do you count?
options: six, with fear of the Lord twice.
fork.reveal: the Hebrew has six, with fear of the Lord repeated. the Greek and Latin rendered one as piety, and the Church's list became seven.

original.note: Hebrew: branch, shoot. The netser that grows out of Jesse's roots in Isaiah 11:1.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of virtues to work on.
what it means: gifts that rest fully on the promised king, whom Christians see as Christ, and that the Church teaches are given to every Christian in confirmation.
what a scholar hears: the Hebrew lists six, repeating fear of the Lord; the Septuagint and Vulgate render the first as eusebeia and pietas, making seven.

notes: The Douay renders the sixth spirit 'godliness' (Vulgate pietas); the Church's list says 'piety'. Both used. Confirm.
Six vs seven: the Hebrew repeats yir'at YHWH (11:2 and 11:3); the Septuagint has eusebeia in 11:2 and phobos theou in 11:3. Confirm.
CCC 1830–1831 on the seven gifts as permanent dispositions; the link to confirmation is from CCC 1303. Confirm the wording 'sealed especially in confirmation'.
Isaiah 11:1–10 is the first reading for the Second Sunday of Advent, Year A; confirm.
The popular phrase 'the lion shall lie down with the lamb' is not in Isaiah 11; described as a common misquotation.
